case_study_insert.main_stem: Trailhead Outfitters (TRO) is a private limited company in the outdoor and sportswear retail sector, based in Denver, Colorado, employing a workforce of 85. Founded in 2008 by Tom Herrera, it sells hiking and camping gear through six stores and online, operating a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. TRO plans to invest $920,000 in automated conveyor and sorting technology at its distribution centre, financed by a $540,000 hire purchase agreement and a $380,000 bank overdraft. The business has fixed costs of $385,000 a year, a variable cost of $27.50 a unit and a selling price of $45.00, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. TRO faces a picking error rate of 4.6% at its distribution centre, driving wrong-item despatches.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Distribution Centre, Week 42 2026: Picked 9,400 cartons; 433 mispicks were logged, a 4.6% error rate, down from 6.1% in Week 12. Average despatch time is 2.1 days. Overtime reached 126 hours, up 18% ahead of the festive peak. Returns processed this month: 512 units, of which 55% were wrong-item shipments. The latest stock accuracy audit passed at 96.2%, and carrier-damage claims fell to 0.8% of despatches.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Trailhead Outfitters as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate to 5.25%, increasing the cost of variable-rate borrowing such as overdrafts. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by just 2.0% to $12.60 per hour from April 2027, the smallest rise in a decade. (3) Technical textile and ripstop fabric costs rose 9.6% year-on-year and diesel prices rose 11.0%, while consumer spending on outdoor recreation grew 4.2%.

questions.question_text: TRO plans to fund the distribution centre automation with hire purchase and a bank overdraft. Explain two advantages for TRO of using hire purchase to fund the expansion instead of increasing the overdraft.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $540,000 cost of the conveyor and sorting machinery across fixed monthly instalments, making payments predictable and easy to budget against the $385,000 annual fixed costs. An overdraft, by contrast, is repayable on demand and its interest rate moves with the base rate — now 5.25% — so overdraft costs could escalate unpredictably and the bank could withdraw the facility exactly when TRO needs working capital most.

Point 2: Once TRO completes the instalments it will own the automated technology, turning a planned acquisition into a structured purchase without ever paying the full $920,000 at once. The overdraft remains free as a buffer for stock and payroll, and the hire purchase charge matches the long, productive life of the automation. An overdraft would add no ownership, would sit as a permanent short-term liability and would deepen cash-flow strain while the centre is commissioned and picking errors take time to fall below 4.6%.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to TRO's automation investment, financing mix and operating costs.

questions.question_text: TRO is launching next-day delivery for outdoor gear ordered online. Consider sponsorship of national hiking events, advertising in outdoor magazines or a national television campaign. Which should TRO choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Sponsorship of national hiking events: Sponsoring marked trails or entry packs at the national hiking festival places TRO directly in front of exactly the people who buy hiking and camping gear, creates hands-on product experience and generates social media content from participants. It is measurable via event promo codes, far cheaper than television, and the 4.2% growth in outdoor recreation spending shows the audience is expanding. Its limits are seasonal timing and modest reach beyond the participants.

Outdoor magazine advertising: Print ads in hiking and camping titles reach a defined enthusiast audience with high dwell time and editorial credibility, at moderate cost. However, circulation is small and static, frequency is limited to issue dates, and responses are hard to measure — better for reinforcing brand awareness than for a launch-time sales surge tied to the next-day delivery promise.

National television campaign: Television would build the widest national awareness of next-day delivery very quickly and give TRO the perceived national scale of larger chains. But production and airtime costs are very high for a single distribution centre rollout, much of the audience lies outside TRO's six-store catchment or does not buy outdoor gear online, and the wasted impressions would be hard to justify while $920,000 is still being invested and picking errors run at 4.6%.

Recommendation: TRO should choose sponsorship of national hiking events. It is the only option that reaches the exact target market at the moment of maximum receptivity, at a cost TRO can afford, with measurable promo-code responses and rich content for social media. Outdoor magazines are rejected as too narrow and slow for a launch, national television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a distributor still commissioning $920,000 of automation rather than rolling out nationally.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the three promotional options with minimal application to TRO.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of TRO with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of TRO with a well-justified recommendation explaining why magazines and television are rejected.

questions.question_text: TRO's distribution centre is logging a 4.6% picking error rate. Explain two benefits for TRO of using autocratic leadership to tackle this problem with its warehouse team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership provides clear, non-negotiable standard operating procedures — scan-check every carton at every bay, barcode verification before despatch — with no ambiguity about expectations. Fast top-down decisions on shift patterns and error hotspots are exactly what a 4.6% mispick rate needs, and consistent discipline cuts errors quickly rather than waiting for consensus, protecting the 96.2% stock accuracy already achieved at audit.

Point 2: Close supervision lets supervisors intervene the moment an error appears, retrain on the spot and prevent recurrence — reducing the 433 mispicks logged in Week 42 and the 55% wrong-item share of the 512 monthly returns. In a safety-critical environment around automated conveyors, autocratic control also enforces rules without debate, reducing accident risk and protecting the 85 employees while the new $920,000 technology is installed and goes live.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to TRO's picking errors, operations log and warehouse environment.

questions.question_text: TRO must train 22 conveyor and sorting-line operators on the new technology. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at an accredited automation college. Which should TRO choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Learning alongside experienced operators keeps the 22 trainees productive, is directly relevant to TRO's specific conveyors and sorting software, costs no tuition fees and reinforces the standard procedures that reduce the 4.6% mispick rate. Drawbacks are that trainers are removed from their own duties at a time when overtime is already up 18%, bad habits can transfer, and there is no formal certificate — a problem for insurers once $920,000 of automated equipment is running at full speed.

Off-the-job training: An accredited college course teaches conveyor mechanics, software diagnostics and machinery safety in a distraction-free environment and ends with a recognised certificate for all 22 operators, valuable evidence for insurers and for compliance around automated machinery. Drawbacks are tuition fees (roughly $1,250 per employee, about $27,500 in total), time away from the distribution centre during the festive peak, and content generic to the industry rather than TRO's exact configuration.

Decision: TRO should choose off-the-job training first, followed by brief on-the-job consolidation. The $920,000 investment is too valuable and the safety stakes too high to rely on informal learning around live conveyors; a certificate also protects TRO commercially and with its insurers. On-the-job training alone is rejected because it embeds unverified habits around dangerous, expensive machinery and leaves TRO unable to evidence operator competence. Once the core course is complete, short on-the-job sessions tailored to TRO's warehouse can follow at minimal extra cost.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of on-the-job and off-the-job training with limited application to TRO.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of TRO.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of TRO with a well-justified decision covering cost, safety and the new technology.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TRO's management can use its cost, contribution and break-even data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $45.00 − $27.50 = $17.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $17.50.
Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $385,000 ÷ ($45.00 − $27.50) = $385,000 ÷ $17.50 = 22,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 22,000 units a year.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TRO's management can use this contribution and break-even data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. TRO can check that 40,000 units exceed the 22,000-unit break-even output, confirming a margin of safety of 18,000 units before committing $920,000 to the conveyor investment.
2. Contribution per unit of $17.50 lets managers model online promotions, such as 10% off at $40.50 cutting contribution to $13.00, to test whether filling the new conveyors to capacity still covers fixed costs.
3. Break-even output supports the financing review: the centre must sell well above 22,000 units a year to service the $540,000 hire purchase instalments and the $380,000 overdraft at 5.25%, informing how fast TRO can repay both.
4. Unit cost data ($385,000 ÷ 40,000 units + $27.50 = $37.125, about $37.13) benchmarks performance every quarter, supports tighter control of the 4.6% mispick rate and 433 weekly errors, and sharpens negotiations with fabric suppliers amid the 9.6% textile cost rise.

questions.model_answer: (i) Contribution per unit = $17.50 | (ii) Break-even output = 22,000 units | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 18,000 units; online promotion modelling at $17.50 contribution; hire purchase and overdraft feasibility for the $540,000 plan; unit-cost benchmarking at $37.125 a unit to cut the 4.6% error rate and negotiate the 9.6% textile increase.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TRO's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TRO's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.45 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.52 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.91 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.06 : 1

Detailed workings: Current assets 2024 = $150,000 inventories + $210,000 trade receivables + $40,000 cash = $400,000. Current assets 2025 = $120,000 + $240,000 + $35,000 = $395,000. Short-term cover 2024 = $400,000 ÷ $275,000 = 1.45; 2025 = $395,000 ÷ $260,000 = 1.52. Stricter measure 2024 = ($400,000 − $150,000) ÷ $275,000 = $250,000 ÷ $275,000 = 0.91; 2025 = ($395,000 − $120,000) ÷ $260,000 = $275,000 ÷ $260,000 = 1.06.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. Short-term cover rose from 1.45 to 1.52 and the stricter measure climbed from 0.91 to 1.06, lifting TRO above covering short-term debts without selling stock — reassuring while it carries hire purchase instalments and a $380,000 overdraft at 5.25%. Inventories fell from $150,000 to $120,000, consistent with a faster distribution model and the push to cut despatch times below 2.1 days. Concerns remain: trade receivables rose from $210,000 to $240,000, tying up an extra month of sales value, and cash fell from $40,000 to $35,000 just as TRO committed to $920,000 of investment — any further slippage in collections could strain the overdraft during peak season.

Conclusion: TRO's financial position has improved. The gains in short-term cover (1.45 to 1.52) and the stricter measure (0.91 to 1.06) outweigh the modest cash fall, and the improvement is supported by leaner inventories and lower current liabilities. TRO should tighten collections of trade receivables and keep overdraft usage below the $380,000 limit so the improvement holds as the new conveyors are commissioned.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether TRO's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TRO of introducing automated conveyor and sorting technology in its distribution centre.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Automation directly attacks the 4.6% picking error rate. Barcode-verified sorting and automated routing should cut mispicks well below the 433 logged in Week 42, protect the 96.2% stock accuracy audit, speed despatch below the current 2.1 days and shrink the 55% wrong-item share of the 512 monthly returns — freeing working capital, delighting the six stores and online channel, and absorbing festive peak volumes without yet more overtime (126 hours, up 18%).

Disadvantage: The technology costs $920,000 and commits TRO to hire purchase instalments plus an overdraft now priced off a 5.25% base rate, adding to fixed costs beyond the $385,000 already carried. Automated systems need 22 operators retrained, specialist maintenance and physical safeguarding; if integration fails or volumes disappoint, TRO faces high fixed charges on inflexible equipment and a de-skilled workforce, and peak-season errors could cascade across the entire network before the benefits are realised.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TRO's conveyor plan, error rate and operating data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.25%, the 2.0% minimum wage increase to $12.60 and the combined 9.6% technical textile cost increase and 11.0% diesel price rise will affect TRO. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (to 5.25%): TRO draws on a $380,000 overdraft, so a rise in the base rate increases its interest charge proportionally — perhaps an extra $1,500 to $3,000 a year depending on average drawn balance. Hire purchase instalments are fixed, limiting further exposure, but carrying trade receivables and stock for longer becomes more expensive, and delaying repayment of the overdraft is costlier than before.

Minimum wage increase (2.0%, to $12.60 per hour): With 85 employees, the 2.0% rise is the smallest in a decade; staffing costs remain manageable, though the longest-serving warehouse staff may still expect progression as they master the new technology.

Technical textile and ripstop fabric costs (+9.6%) and diesel prices (+11.0%): A 9.6% rise on TRO's $27.50 variable cost is about $2.64 per unit ($27.50 × 9.6% = $2.64), squeezing the $17.50 contribution on each of the 40,000 units a year sold; diesel price rises are material but small relative to textile costs and can be passed to carriers through fuel surcharges. TRO must renegotiate fabric contracts, tighten cutting waste and review pricing to defend the $17.50 contribution and the next-day delivery promise.

Conclusion: The 9.6% increase in technical textile costs will have the greatest impact. It erodes the $17.50 contribution on every unit sold and directly threatens the economics of the $920,000 automation investment, while the 11.0% diesel rise is small and passable to carriers and the 2.0% minimum wage rise is the mildest in a decade with manageable staffing costs. TRO must renegotiate fabric contracts, tighten cutting waste, audit carrier surcharges and review pricing to defend margins and the next-day delivery promise.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to TRO.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TRO's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of TRO with a well-justified judgment that textile input costs have the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
